name: Original Practice Test 3
source: Original LSAT-style questions written for LSAT Trainer (harder than the real test). Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Coach Varela has proposed shortening matches in the Ridgefield youth soccer league from sixty minutes to fifty in order to reduce player injuries. Admittedly, shorter matches would mean less total time on the field. Her proposal is nonetheless unlikely to achieve its aim. League records show that the large majority of injuries occur within the first twenty minutes of play, when players' muscles are not yet fully warmed up, and a shorter match would trim time only from the end of play. So the change would leave untouched the very period in which most injuries occur.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Most injuries in the Ridgefield league occur within the first twenty minutes of play, before players are fully warmed up.
Reducing the length of matches is not likely to bring about a meaningful reduction in injuries in the Ridgefield league.
The Ridgefield league should adopt measures to ensure that players are warmed up before play begins.
Shortening matches would leave untouched the period of play in which most injuries in the Ridgefield league occur.
Shorter matches would reduce the total amount of time that Ridgefield players spend on the field.
questions.explanation: The argument's main point is that the proposal is unlikely to achieve its aim of reducing injuries (B). D is the tempting trap: it appears in the last sentence, but it is an intermediate conclusion offered in support of B. A is a premise, E is a concession, and C is never asserted.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Marrow County election officials replaced the county's ballot with a redesigned version featuring larger type and simplified marking instructions. In the election that followed, the proportion of ballots rejected because they were improperly marked fell from 3 percent to under 1 percent. Clearly, then, the redesign must be responsible for this decline in rejected ballots.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on a comparison between elections that were held in different jurisdictions
treats one feature of the redesign as though it were the only feature that changed
draws a conclusion about all voters from a sample of ballots that may be unrepresentative
overlooks the possibility that some other difference between the two elections brought about the decline
takes for granted that improper marking is the only reason a ballot can be rejected
questions.explanation: The argument infers causation simply because the decline followed the redesign, ignoring other changes (different ballot length, voter outreach, a different electorate) that could explain it, so D is correct. E is tempting, but the argument concerns only ballots rejected for improper marking and makes no assumption about other grounds for rejection. A is inaccurate because both elections were in Marrow County.

questions.stimulus: The leaves of the coastal shrub Fenwick's sage are covered with fine hairs. Botanist Ilse Moravec hypothesizes that these hairs help the plant conserve water by trapping a layer of humid air against the leaf surface, thereby slowing evaporation. In support of her hypothesis, she notes that Fenwick's sage plants growing on dry, exposed bluffs have considerably denser leaf hairs than do plants of the same species growing in sheltered, moist ravines.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: When the hairs were removed from leaves of Fenwick's sage, those leaves lost water significantly faster than comparable leaves whose hairs were left intact.
Several other coastal shrubs whose leaves lack hairs grow abundantly on the same dry, exposed bluffs as Fenwick's sage.
Leaf hairs on Fenwick's sage reflect a substantial portion of incoming sunlight, keeping the leaf surface cooler than it would otherwise be.
Fenwick's sage plants on exposed bluffs receive substantially more direct sunlight than do those growing in ravines.
Fenwick's sage grows more slowly in moist ravines than it does on dry, exposed bluffs.
questions.explanation: A directly tests the hypothesized function: removing the hairs speeds water loss, as the hypothesis predicts. C is the main trap: a cooler leaf might lose less water, but C points to a different mechanism (reflecting sunlight) and so offers a rival account of why bluff plants have denser hairs, rather than supporting the humid-air hypothesis. D likewise suggests sun protection as the reason for denser hairs, and B and E do not bear on the hairs' function.

questions.stimulus: Every space heater sold by Halvorsen Appliances has passed the industry's tip-over test, and any heater that passes the tip-over test is equipped with an automatic shutoff switch. Several heaters sold by Halvorsen were recalled last year following customer complaints. However, according to the industry safety board, no heater that was equipped with both an automatic shutoff switch and an overheat sensor was recalled last year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Every heater equipped with an automatic shutoff switch has passed the tip-over test.
No heater sold by Halvorsen Appliances is equipped with an overheat sensor.
Some heaters that have passed the tip-over test were not sold by Halvorsen Appliances.
Every heater that was recalled last year was sold by Halvorsen Appliances.
At least one heater sold by Halvorsen Appliances lacks an overheat sensor.
questions.explanation: Each recalled Halvorsen heater passed the tip-over test and so has a shutoff switch; since no recalled heater had both a switch and an overheat sensor, those recalled heaters must lack an overheat sensor, so E must be true. B is too strong: only the recalled heaters must lack the sensor. A reverses the stated conditional, and C and D go beyond the information given.

questions.stimulus:
Rhee: A scientific theory earns our confidence only by making predictions that could have turned out to be false and did not. A theory that merely accommodates data that had already been collected, however elegantly it does so, has not yet been tested at all.

Lindqvist: That standard is too strict. When a theory accounts for a large body of previously puzzling observations using fewer assumptions than its rivals, that achievement is itself a genuine test the theory has passed, even if the observations were known before the theory was formulated.
questions.stem: Rhee and Lindqvist disagree over whether
choices: a theory that makes successful predictions of new observations deserves some degree of confidence
simpler theories are generally more likely to be true than more complex ones
a theory's accounting for observations made before it was formulated can count as a test of that theory
most scientific theories are formulated only after the observations relevant to them have been made
a theory that makes even one false prediction should be abandoned
questions.explanation: Rhee says accommodating already collected data is no test at all, while Lindqvist says explaining previously known observations can be a genuine test, so they disagree about C. A is a point both would likely accept; Lindqvist does not deny that successful novel predictions earn confidence. Neither speaker addresses B, D, or E.

questions.stimulus: In a recent study, volunteers rated their mood after spending an hour in either a room painted pale blue or a room painted bright orange. On average, those who had been in the blue room reported calmer moods than those who had been in the orange room. The researchers concluded that pale blue surroundings tend to have a calming effect on people. But this conclusion is plainly mistaken. A painter I know has worked in a pale blue studio for years, and she is one of the most agitated people I have ever met.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that it
choices: treats a single case as sufficient to refute a claim about a general tendency
attacks the researchers' character rather than the reasoning behind their conclusion
fails to consider that the volunteers' reports of their own moods may have been inaccurate
presupposes the truth of the very conclusion it is trying to establish
confuses a condition sufficient for calmness with a condition necessary for it
questions.explanation: The researchers claimed only that pale blue surroundings tend to calm people; one agitated painter cannot refute a claim about an average tendency, so A is correct. C is tempting because it names a real weakness of the study, but the arguer's reasoning does not depend on the accuracy of the mood reports; the arguer's error lies in the anecdotal counterexample.

questions.stimulus: The cod population of Tessaly Bay has fallen sharply over the past decade. To reverse this decline, regulators plan to increase the minimum mesh size of trawl nets used in the bay. The larger mesh will allow most juvenile cod that encounter the nets to pass through them unharmed. Since an increase in the number of juvenile cod that survive to reproductive age will boost the population, the new regulation will help reverse the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: The decline in Tessaly Bay's cod population was caused primarily by trawling.
Most juvenile cod that pass through the larger mesh will survive to reproductive age.
No other regulation would reverse the decline more quickly than the new mesh requirement.
At present, a significant number of juvenile cod in Tessaly Bay are caught in trawl nets.
Fishers in Tessaly Bay will not object to the new mesh size requirement.
questions.explanation: If few juvenile cod are currently caught in trawl nets, letting them pass through would not increase juvenile survival, and the argument collapses; so it requires D. A is attractive but too strong: the regulation could help even if trawling were only one of several causes of the decline. B is also too strong, since the argument needs only that more juveniles survive than before, not that most of those escaping do.

questions.stimulus: Building codes in the city of Calder require that buildings constructed after 1990 have far more insulation than was required for buildings constructed earlier. Yet a survey of Calder's office buildings found that, on average, those constructed after 1990 use more energy per square meter for heating and cooling than do those constructed before 1990.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The cost of insulation materials has declined substantially since 1990.
Calder office buildings constructed after 1990 typically have extensive glass facades, which let far more heat pass through than do the masonry walls typical of older buildings.
Some Calder office buildings constructed before 1990 have since been retrofitted with additional insulation.
Residential buildings in Calder constructed after 1990 use less energy for heating than do older residential buildings.
Energy prices in Calder have risen steadily since 1990.
questions.explanation: B identifies a feature of the newer buildings that would increase heat transfer enough to outweigh their extra insulation, explaining their higher energy use. C is tempting, but retrofitting some older buildings would at most bring their insulation closer to that of newer ones; it would not explain why the newer buildings use more energy. D only deepens the puzzle, and A and E affect old and new buildings alike.

questions.stimulus: Sports analyst: Over the past five seasons, Northern League basketball players who wore the new Strata compression sleeves missed, on average, 30 percent fewer games due to injury than did players who did not wear them. This difference is too large to be a matter of chance. Clearly, then, wearing Strata sleeves substantially reduces a player's risk of injury.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Players who began wearing Strata sleeves had missed about as many games to injury in the preceding season as had players who never wore them.
Some players who wore Strata sleeves nonetheless missed many games due to injury.
Compression sleeves of various brands have been shown to increase blood flow to the muscles they cover.
Players who wore Strata sleeves played, on average, more minutes per game than did players who did not wear them.
Northern League trainers generally discouraged players with a history of recurring injuries from using any unproven equipment, including Strata sleeves.
questions.explanation: E weakens the argument by showing the comparison groups were unlike from the start: players prone to injury were steered away from the sleeves, so the sleeve wearers may have missed fewer games simply because they were less injury-prone. A is the main trap but points the wrong way: if wearers had injury records similar to non-wearers before adopting the sleeves, that rules out exactly this selection effect and strengthens the argument. D also strengthens it, since wearers had more exposure to injury yet missed fewer games.

questions.stimulus: Some election administrators argue that allowing voters to register on election day will overwhelm polling-place staff and lengthen lines. This concern is understandable but overstated. In the three states that most recently adopted same-day registration, average waiting times at polling places did not increase measurably in the first election after adoption. Admittedly, those states also hired additional poll workers for that election. But the number of workers they added was small relative to the number of same-day registrants, so the added staff cannot by itself account for the absence of longer lines.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that those states also hired additional poll workers for that election?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion.
It is offered as direct evidence that the administrators' concern is overstated.
It acknowledges a fact that might seem to undermine the argument's evidence, which the argument then contends does not do so.
It is a claim that the argument attempts to show is false.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the number of added workers was small.
questions.explanation: The hiring of additional workers is conceded ('Admittedly') because it could explain the absence of longer lines and so weaken the evidence; the argument then explains why it does not, matching C. D is the trap: the argument never disputes that the workers were hired, only that the hiring accounts for the result. The main conclusion is that the concern is overstated, so A is wrong.

questions.stimulus: Conservation biologist: The orchid Dendra pallida, which is native to the Pellam Highlands, can germinate only in the presence of one particular species of soil fungus. Any plant whose germination depends on a single fungal species is vulnerable to soil disturbance unless its seeds can remain dormant for more than a decade, and no orchid native to the Pellam Highlands produces seeds that can remain dormant that long. Hence Dendra pallida should be included in the regional conservation registry.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: No plant species should be excluded from the regional conservation registry if it is vulnerable to soil disturbance.
Any plant whose germination depends on a single fungal species and whose seeds can remain dormant for more than a decade should be included in the registry.
Every plant species included in the regional conservation registry is vulnerable to soil disturbance.
Only plant species that are vulnerable to soil disturbance should be included in the regional conservation registry.
The seeds of Dendra pallida cannot remain dormant for more than a decade.
questions.explanation: The premises chain together to show that Dendra pallida depends on a single fungus and lacks long-dormant seeds, and so is vulnerable to soil disturbance. A, phrased negatively, says any vulnerable species should not be excluded, that is, should be included, which completes the argument. D is the main trap: it makes vulnerability necessary for inclusion, not sufficient, so it does not yield the conclusion. C reverses the needed conditional, B describes plants unlike Dendra pallida, and E merely restates something already derivable.

questions.stimulus: In an experiment, participants memorized a list of words while seated either in a quiet room or in a room filled with recorded café noise. A day later, each participant was tested for recall in one of the two rooms. Participants who were tested in the same room in which they had memorized the words recalled more words, on average, than participants who were tested in the other room. This was true both for those who had memorized the words in the quiet room and for those who had memorized them in the noisy room.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Quiet surroundings are better suited to memorization than noisy surroundings are.
People who study in noisy surroundings should always be tested in noisy surroundings.
Background noise has no effect on recall when learning and testing take place in the same room.
Most participants recalled more words when they were tested in the quiet room.
Whether the conditions of testing match the conditions of learning can affect how much learned material is recalled.
questions.explanation: Recall was better whenever the test room matched the learning room, regardless of which room it was, which strongly supports E. A and D compare the rooms themselves, which the results do not address. B is far too strong, and C claims an absence of any effect that the data cannot show.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: Some critics argue that because scientific theories have repeatedly been overturned in the past, we should expect our current theories to be overturned as well. But every theory that has been overturned was overturned by scientists applying the scientific method. So the history of overturned theories, far from undermining science, shows that the scientific method is reliable. We may therefore conclude that our current scientific theories are likely to be true.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that some theories may have been overturned by means other than the scientific method
moves from a claim about the reliability of a method for correcting theories to a conclusion about the truth of the theories that method currently supports
relies on the authority of scientists rather than on evidence about the theories themselves
treats the fact that past theories have been overturned as evidence that current theories will also be overturned
draws a conclusion that merely restates one of the premises offered in its support
questions.explanation: The premises show at most that the scientific method reliably corrects errors; that is compatible with current theories also being overturned later, so the argument illegitimately concludes they are likely true (B). D is a trap: that inference belongs to the critics, which the philosopher rejects rather than commits. A is wrong because the argument states as a premise that every overturned theory was overturned by the scientific method, and accepting a premise is not a flaw.

questions.stimulus: A manufacturer that learns of a hazard in one of its products is obligated to warn consumers promptly if the hazard could cause serious injury and consumers could not reasonably be expected to discover the hazard on their own. If either of these conditions is not met, the manufacturer may decide whether to issue a warning on the basis of other considerations.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Pinewood Furniture learned that the finish on one of its chairs can cause a mild, temporary rash, a hazard consumers could not detect in advance. So Pinewood was obligated to warn consumers promptly.

Marlo Housewares learned that the handle of one of its kettles can get hot enough to cause serious burns, a fact made evident before use by a prominent label and by steam that visibly vents beside the handle. So Marlo was obligated to warn consumers promptly.

Ostrander Ladders learned that rungs on one of its ladders can crack without any visible sign, risking serious falls. Since Ostrander had already stopped selling that ladder, it was not obligated to warn consumers.

Trevlan Tools learned that the blade guard on one of its saws can detach, risking severe cuts, and that the loosening cannot be detected without disassembling the saw. So Trevlan was obligated to warn consumers promptly.
Quella Toys learned that small magnets in one of its toys could cause serious internal injuries if swallowed, a hazard consumers could not detect. So Quella was obligated to recall the toy.
questions.explanation: In D the hazard could cause serious injury and cannot reasonably be discovered by consumers, so both conditions are met and the obligation to warn applies. E is the strongest trap: both conditions are met, but the principle requires only a prompt warning, not a recall. C is also tempting, but whether the ladder is still sold is irrelevant; both conditions are met, so a warning was obligatory. In A the hazard is not serious, and in B it is readily discoverable.

questions.stimulus: To protect the declining population of salmon in the Arden River, the regional fisheries board closed the river's lower reaches to recreational fishing three years ago. Since then, the number of adult salmon returning to the Arden River to spawn has risen by 40 percent. The board's director concludes that the fishing closure is responsible for this increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: whether most recreational fishers in the region support the closure
whether the Arden River salmon population had been declining for more than a decade before the closure
whether the number of adult salmon returning to spawn in nearby rivers that remained open to fishing also rose over the same period
whether salmon are the species most sought by recreational fishers on the Arden River
whether the fisheries board intends to extend the closure to the river's upper reaches
questions.explanation: If salmon returns rose similarly in nearby rivers that stayed open, some regional factor rather than the closure probably explains the increase; if they did not, the director's conclusion gains support. So C is the most useful to know. B is tempting but concerns only the history of the decline, not what caused the recent increase; A, D, and E are irrelevant to the causal claim.

questions.stimulus: Race official: Every cyclist who receives a starting position in the Barrow Classic must both have registered by Friday and have completed at least two regional races this season. Ilona registered on Thursday, but she has completed only one regional race this season. Therefore, Ilona will not receive a starting position in the Barrow Classic.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Any building approved for the historic tax credit must both have been built before 1920 and retain its original facade. The Marston Building was built in 1905, but its facade was replaced in 1980. So the Marston Building will not be approved for the credit.
Every applicant hired by the firm must both hold a degree and have two years of experience. Petra holds a degree and has two years of experience. So Petra will be hired by the firm.

If a student both attends every lecture and completes every problem set, she will pass the course. Dara attended every lecture but did not complete every problem set. So Dara will not pass the course.
Only residents who have lived in the town for a year and own property there may vote on the levy. Gerald has voted on the levy. So Gerald must own property in the town.
Every successful bakery in the city both uses local flour and opens before 7 a.m. The Copper Loaf uses local flour and opens before 7 a.m. So the Copper Loaf is successful.
questions.explanation: The original states two necessary conditions for an outcome, shows that the subject meets one but fails the other, and validly concludes the outcome will not occur; A matches this exactly. C looks similar but treats the two conditions as sufficient, so concluding failure from missing one is a flawed denial of a sufficient condition. B and E wrongly infer the outcome from its necessary conditions, and D infers a condition from the outcome.

questions.stimulus: Architectural historian: The nave of the cathedral at Vessan is about two meters wider at its western end than at its eastern end. Some scholars attribute this to deliberate design: the narrowing would make the nave appear longer to someone entering through the main doors at the west. More likely, however, the tapering resulted from measurement error. The nave was built over sixty years by successive crews, beginning at the eastern end, and builders of that era commonly laid out foundations section by section using ropes that stretched in humid weather.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Ropes used by builders of that era were often made of fibers that stretch less than most other fibers available at the time.
Several cathedrals built in the same era were deliberately designed to create optical illusions for visitors.
Careful measurements show that the nave of the Vessan cathedral narrows at a steady, uniform rate along its entire length from west to east.
When viewed from the western doors, the nave of the Vessan cathedral does appear noticeably longer than it actually is.
The width of the nave does not change gradually but shifts abruptly at several points that coincide with the boundaries between sections built by different crews.
questions.explanation: A deliberate optical design would produce a smooth taper, whereas abrupt shifts at the boundaries between crews' sections are just what section-by-section measurement error would produce, so E strengthens the historian's view. C is the subtlest trap: it looks like confirming evidence about the taper, but a steady, uniform narrowing is the signature of a planned design and therefore weakens the argument. D likewise supports the rival optical-illusion explanation, and A and B also tend to weaken the argument.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: A colleague claims that our finding, namely that people who are told a task is difficult persist at it longer than people who are told it is easy, is merely an artifact of our having used university students as participants. But if that were so, then repeating the experiment with participants drawn from a broader population should have eliminated the effect. We conducted exactly such a repetition, with participants recruited from community centers in three cities, and the effect was, if anything, stronger.
questions.stem: The researcher's argument proceeds by
choices: questioning the colleague's qualifications to evaluate the experiment
showing that the colleague's hypothesis implies a prediction that, when tested, turned out to be false
offering an alternative explanation of the finding that the colleague failed to consider
arguing that because the colleague's claim has not been proven, it must be false
showing that the colleague's hypothesis is inconsistent with the original finding it was proposed to explain
questions.explanation: The researcher derives a prediction from the colleague's hypothesis (a broader sample would eliminate the effect), tests it, and reports that it failed, which is B. E is the trap: the hypothesis conflicts with the result of the new replication, not with the original finding, which it was designed to explain away. The researcher does not offer a rival explanation of the finding (C) or attack the colleague's qualifications (A).

questions.stimulus: Election commissioner: In our county, voters who cast ballots by mail must sign the return envelope, and that signature is compared with the one on file. In the last election, 2 percent of mail ballots here were rejected for signature mismatches, far more than in neighboring counties. Our staff are no less careful than staff elsewhere, so the high rejection rate is most likely due to the age of the signatures on file: a person's signature often changes over time, and unlike neighboring counties, we never ask voters to update their signatures.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The signatures of older voters change more over time than do those of younger voters.
Neighboring counties ask voters to update their signatures on file at least once a year.
Most voters in the commissioner's county cast their ballots by mail.
The proportion of mail ballots in the commissioner's county that were signed by someone other than the voter is not much greater than it is in neighboring counties.
If the county began asking voters to update their signatures, its rejection rate would fall below that of neighboring counties.
questions.explanation: If far more ballots in the county were actually signed by someone other than the voter, genuine mismatches rather than outdated signatures would explain the high rejection rate, so the argument requires D. B is too specific: the argument needs only that neighboring counties ask for updates, not how often. E is too strong; the argument does not require that the rate fall below that of neighboring counties.

questions.stimulus: Marine biologist: Lobster harvests off the coast of Brennick Island have fallen by half over the past eight years. During the same period, the water temperature off the island has risen by about 1.5 degrees Celsius. Laboratory studies show that lobster larvae raised in water 1.5 degrees warmer than the island's historical average have markedly lower survival rates. So the warming of the island's waters is the main cause of the decline in the lobster harvest.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Lobster harvests have also declined in some regions where water temperatures have remained stable.
Adult lobsters can tolerate increases in water temperature considerably larger than 1.5 degrees Celsius.
Eight years ago, the number of boats licensed to harvest lobster off Brennick Island was cut in half, and the catch per boat has remained nearly constant since then.
Water temperatures off Brennick Island have fluctuated considerably over previous centuries.
Lobster larvae that survive to adulthood off Brennick Island grow somewhat faster in warmer water.
questions.explanation: If half the boats were removed and each boat's catch stayed constant, the halving of the harvest is fully explained by reduced fishing effort, not by fewer lobsters, which severely weakens the argument (C). A is attractive but shows only that something else can cause declines elsewhere; it says nothing about the cause at Brennick Island. B concerns adults, whereas the argument relies on larval survival.

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: The Kelby company's new electric bicycle battery has passed every safety test that regulators currently require. Nevertheless, Kelby should delay releasing it. Independent engineers have identified a plausible mechanism by which the battery could overheat during prolonged charging in hot weather, a condition that the required tests do not simulate, and Kelby has not yet investigated whether this overheating actually occurs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: Regulators should revise their required safety tests whenever engineers identify a hazard that those tests do not simulate.
A product that has passed all required safety tests should be presumed safe unless it has been shown to cause harm.
A company should delay releasing a product whenever it has confirmed that the product can overheat under conditions that required safety tests do not simulate.
A company should delay releasing a product only if it has confirmed that the product poses a hazard to consumers.
A company should not release a product while a credible potential hazard not addressed by required tests remains uninvestigated, even if the product meets all regulatory requirements.
questions.explanation: The advocate concludes that Kelby should delay release because a credible, untested hazard has not been investigated, despite regulatory compliance; E states exactly that principle. C is the closest trap, but it applies only once overheating has been confirmed, and Kelby has not confirmed anything, which is the advocate's very point. A addresses what regulators should do, not Kelby, and B and D point toward releasing the battery.

questions.stimulus: In the alpine meadows of the Corvin range, the wildflower Lessia nivalis produces two kinds of flowers: showy flowers that must be pollinated by bumblebees, and small closed flowers that pollinate themselves. In years when bumblebees are scarce, Lessia plants produce a higher proportion of closed flowers. Researchers have found that Lessia plants fix the proportion of each flower type within the first two weeks after snowmelt, whereas bumblebees in the Corvin range do not emerge from hibernation until at least a month after snowmelt. Years of bumblebee scarcity in the range are reliably preceded by cold, late springs.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The proportion of closed flowers that a Lessia plant produces is probably determined by some cue other than the presence of bumblebees in the meadow that season.
In years when bumblebees are plentiful, Lessia plants in the Corvin range produce no closed flowers.
Lessia plants grown from the seeds of closed flowers produce fewer showy flowers than do other Lessia plants.
A cold, late spring causes bumblebee populations in the Corvin range to decline.
Showy Lessia flowers produce more seeds per flower than closed Lessia flowers do.
questions.explanation: Lessia fixes its flower proportions before any bumblebees have emerged, yet the proportions track bumblebee scarcity, so the plants must be responding to some other cue, such as spring conditions; this supports A. D is the main trap: the passage says only that cold, late springs reliably precede bumblebee scarcity, not that they cause it. B is too strong, and C and E are not addressed.

questions.stimulus: City planner: No building in the Harrow district may exceed six stories unless it has received a variance from the zoning board. The board grants variances only to projects that include ground-floor retail space, and it grants no variance to any project that would reduce the number of on-street parking spaces. The proposed Linwood Tower, in the Harrow district, would exceed six stories and would include ground-floor retail space, but its loading dock would eliminate four on-street parking spaces. Therefore, the Linwood Tower will not be built as proposed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Most projects that the zoning board has denied a variance were later revised and then approved.
No building will be built as proposed if, as proposed, it could not lawfully be built in the Harrow district.
The zoning board grants a variance to every project that includes ground-floor retail space.
The developers of the Linwood Tower will not revise their plans in order to preserve the four parking spaces.
The Linwood Tower will not receive a variance from the zoning board.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that the tower as proposed exceeds six stories and cannot receive a variance (it would eliminate parking), so it could not lawfully be built as proposed; B links that to its not being built as proposed. E is a trap because it is already derivable from the premises and does not connect unlawfulness to what will be built. D is tempting, but the conclusion concerns the plan as proposed, so possible revisions are beside the point. C ignores the parking restriction and, in any case, does not close the gap.

questions.stimulus: Sports journalist: Most of the players on the Kestrel Rovers' current roster are over thirty years old, and most players in the league who are over thirty have suffered a serious injury at some point in their careers. It follows that most of the Rovers' current players have suffered a serious injury at some point in their careers.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: All members of the Fenwick hiking club are over thirty, and all people over thirty in the region have hiked the coastal trail. So all members of the Fenwick hiking club have hiked the coastal trail.
Most residents of Pell Street own a dog, and most residents of Pell Street walk at least an hour a day. So most of the residents of Pell Street who own a dog walk at least an hour a day.
Some employees of Darrow Consulting speak French, and some people who speak French have lived abroad. So some employees of Darrow Consulting have lived abroad.
Most residents of Pell Street own a dog, and most dog owners in the city walk at least an hour a day. So most residents of Pell Street walk at least an hour a day.
Most of the paintings in the Ostrow Gallery are oil paintings, and every oil painting in the gallery was donated. So most of the paintings in the Ostrow Gallery were donated.
questions.explanation: The original chains two 'most' statements (most A are B; most B are C) to conclude that most A are C, which does not follow; D repeats this exact pattern. C is the strongest trap, since it also chains overlapping groups invalidly, but it uses 'some' rather than 'most' and so is less similar. A and E are valid, and B commits a different error about the overlap of two groups.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: According to a widely accepted criterion, a hypothesis counts as scientific only if some possible observation would show it to be false. Dr. Amsel's hypothesis about the formation of the Tarvo crater clearly satisfies this requirement, since she has specified precisely which mineral deposits, if they were discovered at the site, would refute her hypothesis. So, by that criterion, Amsel's hypothesis qualifies as scientific.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that a criterion is correct merely because it is widely accepted
fails to establish that the mineral deposits Amsel specified have not in fact been found at the site
treats a condition that the criterion requires of a scientific hypothesis as if it were enough to make a hypothesis scientific
takes for granted that a hypothesis that could be refuted is likely to be refuted
relies on Amsel's own description of her hypothesis without considering how other scientists would describe it
questions.explanation: The criterion states only a necessary condition ('only if'), but the argument concludes that meeting it makes the hypothesis scientific, treating the necessary condition as sufficient (C). A is tempting, but the conclusion is explicitly limited to what follows 'by that criterion,' so the argument does not assume the criterion is correct. B is irrelevant because falsifiability depends on what could be observed, not on what has been found.

passages.title: Output restriction at a seasonal cannery
passages.text:
For much of the past half century, labor historians have treated the deliberate restriction of output by piece-rate workers as a form of quiet resistance. Workers paid by the unit, the account runs, learned that whenever their earnings rose noticeably, management would lower the rate paid per piece, and so they agreed among themselves to cap production at a level that would not invite a cut. Output restriction was thus understood as a defensive bargain struck against employers, and its prevalence was read as evidence of a solidarity that cut across ethnic and craft divisions within the workforce.

The historian Tamsin Reyval has challenged this interpretation using the unusually complete payroll ledgers of the Orlen Bay cannery, which processed fish along a northern coast between 1898 and 1931. The ledgers confirm that informal output ceilings were widespread. Yet the cannery’s posted piece rates were almost never reduced during the period, even in years when average earnings climbed sharply. One might reply that workers feared cuts regardless, having heard of them at other plants; a threat need not materialize to shape behavior. But Reyval observes that ceilings at Orlen Bay loosened precisely in the years of unusually heavy runs—the years in which earnings, and so presumably the danger of a cut, were greatest. Workers anxious about rates would have done the reverse.

Reyval’s alternative turns on the seasonal character of the work. The cannery operated only while the fish were running, and it laid off its workers as soon as the season’s catch had been processed. Any worker who produced quickly was therefore shortening the period during which she and her coworkers would be paid. Ceilings were most rigid late in the season, when the remaining catch was small, and loosened in heavy-run years, when no amount of speed could exhaust the supply before the season’s natural close. Restriction, on this reading, was less a contest with management over the price of labor than an arrangement among workers to stretch a fixed quantity of work across as many paid days as possible.

Reyval does not claim that her findings overturn the older view everywhere; plants with year-round production and a record of rate cuts may well have fostered the defensive restriction earlier historians described. Her more general point is methodological: historians inferred motives from the bare fact of restriction and then read those motives back into the evidence. That point seems to me well taken, though her own account is open to a version of the same objection. Ledgers record what workers did, not why, and the pattern Reyval finds shows that the seasonal motive was operative, not that it was the only one. Her study thus establishes less than she sometimes suggests. It nonetheless establishes something the older consensus never allowed for: that identical conduct can answer to quite different pressures, so that the meaning of a practice cannot be settled until the conditions under which it arose have been reconstructed.

passages.title: Early leaf shedding in drought
passages.text:
Passage A

During severe droughts, the pale ridge oak, a deciduous tree of dry upland forests, often drops much of its foliage weeks before the usual autumn leaf fall. Many observers have taken this as a sign of distress, but I believe it is better understood as a defensive strategy. A tree loses water chiefly through its leaves, and as soil moisture declines, the tension in the water columns inside the xylem—the tissue that conducts water upward—increases. Past a certain threshold, air bubbles form in the conducting vessels and block them. Such embolisms in the trunk and major branches are difficult to repair and can kill a tree outright. By shedding leaves, the oak sharply reduces the water it loses, easing the tension on the vessels of its stem.

Leaves, in this view, act as a kind of hydraulic fuse: an inexpensive, replaceable part sacrificed to protect an expensive, irreplaceable one. My colleagues and I monitored two hundred pale ridge oaks through the driest summer of the past decade. Trees that shed more than half their leaves before midsummer had, on average, far fewer blocked vessels in their trunks than trees that retained their foliage, and they were substantially more likely to leaf out normally the following spring. Admittedly, in the most extreme droughts some leaves surely wither and fall because they have failed outright; but a response that is sometimes overwhelmed is not thereby shown to be no response at all.

Passage B

That drought-stressed trees such as the pale ridge oak drop leaves early is not in dispute; what is disputed is whether shedding is a strategy or a consequence. Leaves typically have narrower margins of hydraulic safety than stems, meaning that their conducting vessels become blocked at lower levels of tension. When we measured water flow in the leaves of pale ridge oaks shortly before they fell, we found that most had already lost the large majority of their conducting capacity. Shedding, then, generally follows hydraulic failure in the leaf rather than preventing it. That the stem benefits from reduced water loss once the leaves are gone is real enough, but a benefit that follows from damage is not evidence that the damage was a design.

I do not doubt that early-shedding trees often look healthier the following spring. But a single year’s survival is not a reliable measure of a trait’s value. A tree that discards its canopy in midsummer forgoes weeks of photosynthesis and must draw on stored carbohydrates to build new leaves. In our long-term plots, oaks that shed early in two or more consecutive drought years showed steadily declining reserves of stored starch, and many died within five years—not from blocked vessels but from what appears to be carbon starvation. Whether early leaf loss helps a tree, therefore, depends on how often drought returns, and as droughts in the region become more frequent, a response that once bought time may increasingly exhaust it.

passages.title: The shared-shortage rule
passages.text:
Under the doctrine of prior appropriation, which governs water in much of the arid western United States, the first person to divert water and put it to beneficial use acquires a right senior to those of all later claimants. In a shortage, senior holders take their full allotment before junior holders receive anything. The doctrine’s defenders have long praised its clarity: every user knows exactly where he or she stands in line, and the security of senior rights encourages long-term investment in farms and towns. Its critics reply that the same clarity can be ruinous, since in a dry year a junior user may lose all access to water while a nearby senior user irrigates as usual.

In 1958 the water authority of the Tessaly River basin attempted a compromise. Under what came to be called the shared-shortage rule, any shortfall in a given year was divided among all rights holders in proportion to their allotments, with a single exception: rights used for household drinking water were exempt from reduction. Priority dates were retained, but they were consulted only to settle disputes over the size of allotments, not to determine who would bear a shortage. The rule’s architects argued that spreading losses would prevent the sudden collapse of junior farms and that the predictability seniors valued would survive, since every user could still calculate any shortfall in advance.

A growing body of commentary now contends that the rule’s effects have been less benign than its architects anticipated. Because no user ever loses all of his or her water, the rule removed the strongest incentive junior users had to invest in storage or conservation: a farmer facing a twenty percent cut can usually absorb it by fallowing a field, while one facing a total cutoff must find another source or go out of business. Meanwhile, senior holders, who under strict priority would have been largely insulated from shortage, found their rights exposed to reduction in every dry year. The uncertainty this introduced made those rights harder to value, and transfers of water to growing municipalities, which depend on reliable valuation, slowed considerably. The result, critics argue, is a basin that uses water much as it did in 1958, though its economy has changed dramatically.

Defenders of the rule reply that these criticisms measure it against a standard it was never meant to meet. The rule was designed to distribute hardship fairly, not to maximize the efficiency of water use, and on its own terms it has largely succeeded: no community in the basin has lost its farms in a single season. This is not a trivial achievement, and nothing in the critics’ case shows that a return to strict priority would be wise. Yet the defenders’ reply concedes more than its proponents may intend. A rule that preserves existing patterns of use by softening every shortage may simply defer the reckoning that strict priority would force, leaving the basin less prepared when a drought arrives that no proportional cut can absorb.

passages.title: Reduction and ornament in tonal analysis
passages.text:
Among the most influential methods for analyzing tonal music is what may broadly be called reductive analysis. The analyst begins with the full musical surface—every note in the score—and proceeds by stages to strip away those notes judged to be embellishments: passing tones, neighbor notes, suspensions, and the like. What remains at each stage is a simpler progression, and at the final stage a skeleton of a few structurally essential pitches and harmonies is said to underlie the entire work. The appeal of the method is considerable. It explains how a long movement can be heard as a coherent whole, and it gives precise content to the intuition that some notes matter more than others.

Yet the method rests on a decision it rarely examines: the decision about which notes count as embellishment. In many cases the decision seems obvious; a brief note moving stepwise between two chord tones is almost universally heard as decorative. But in many others it is not, and here analysts typically appeal to the very structure that the reduction is supposed to reveal. A note is classified as ornamental because it does not belong to the underlying progression, and the underlying progression is identified by setting aside the notes classified as ornamental. The circle is not necessarily vicious—interpretation often proceeds by such mutual adjustment—but it means that the skeleton the analyst uncovers is partly a product of the analyst’s prior expectations about what a skeleton should look like.

A further difficulty concerns the status of ornament itself. Reductive analysis treats embellishment as, by definition, inessential: the work would remain recognizably the same work were the ornaments removed. In several performance traditions, however, ornaments were not fixed by the composer but supplied by performers, who varied them from one performance to the next, and listeners in these traditions often judged a performance chiefly by the inventiveness of its ornamentation. For such music, to call ornament inessential is not a neutral analytic observation but a substantive claim about where the music’s value lies—one that the music’s original audiences might well have rejected.

None of this requires abandoning reduction. The method remains an illuminating way of describing one dimension of tonal coherence. What it requires is a more modest account of what reduction achieves. Rather than revealing the structure of a work, a reduction offers one hearing of it, shaped by choices that could have been made otherwise. Analysts who present their reductions in this way—stating, wherever the classification of a note is contested, why they classified it as they did—would sacrifice some of the method’s apparent authority. They would gain, in exchange, an account of musical structure that acknowledges the listener’s part in making it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Reyval’s study of the Orlen Bay ledgers shows that the older account of output restriction as a defense against rate cuts was mistaken.
Labor historians have overstated the degree to which piece-rate workers shared a solidarity that cut across ethnic and craft divisions.

Reyval’s evidence undercuts the rate-cut explanation of output restriction at Orlen Bay and supports her methodological claim, even though it does not show that seasonal pressure was the workers’ sole motive.
Output restriction among piece-rate workers was generally a response to seasonal layoffs rather than to the threat of reduced piece rates.
Because ledgers record only what workers did, Reyval’s account of output restriction at Orlen Bay is no better supported than the account it seeks to replace.
questions.explanation: The passage presents Reyval’s case against the rate-cut explanation at Orlen Bay, endorses her methodological point, and qualifies her account as establishing less than she suggests; C captures all three. A is the main trap: it generalizes beyond Orlen Bay, although the last paragraph says Reyval does not claim to overturn the older view everywhere. E overstates the author’s reservation, since the author says her study establishes something the older consensus never allowed for.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Orlen Bay ledgers show that
choices: output ceilings loosened in years when the fish runs were unusually heavy
output ceilings were most strictly observed in the years when earnings were highest
workers who exceeded informal output ceilings were laid off before their coworkers
posted piece rates were lowered at the close of seasons with unusually heavy runs
output ceilings were most rigidly observed early in the canning season
questions.explanation: Both the second and third paragraphs state that ceilings loosened in heavy-run years, so A is correct. B is the trap: heavy-run years were the years of highest earnings, and the passage says ceilings loosened, not tightened, then. E reverses the statement that ceilings were most rigid late in the season.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that Reyval would most likely agree with which one of the following?
choices: Output restriction at plants with year-round production was motivated chiefly by solidarity among workers of different crafts.
Workers at Orlen Bay were unaware that piece rates at the cannery were seldom lowered.
At a year-round plant with a record of rate cuts, output ceilings would tend to loosen in years of unusually high earnings.
The payroll ledgers of plants with year-round production are less complete than those of the Orlen Bay cannery.
At a cannery whose season ended on a fixed date no matter how quickly the catch was processed, the motive for restriction she identifies would be weaker.
questions.explanation: Reyval’s seasonal motive depends on fast work exhausting the catch and so hastening layoffs, and the ledgers show restriction loosening when speed could not end the season early; with a fixed end date, speed would not shorten paid work, so E follows. C is the trap: it borrows the heavy-run pattern from Orlen Bay, but Reyval argues that workers anxious about rates would have done the reverse, tightening ceilings when earnings rose.

questions.stem: The author mentions the possibility that workers ‘feared cuts regardless, having heard of them at other plants’ primarily in order to
choices: support the older consensus with evidence drawn from plants other than Orlen Bay
raise an objection to one step in Reyval’s reasoning that the passage then reports her answering
suggest that Orlen Bay workers were better informed about other plants than earlier historians assumed
introduce the reservation about Reyval’s account that the author develops in the final paragraph
explain why the posted piece rates at Orlen Bay were almost never reduced
questions.explanation: The sentence anticipates a reply to Reyval’s point that rates were rarely cut, and the next sentences give her answer based on the heavy-run years, so B is correct. D is tempting because the author does voice a reservation later, but that reservation concerns whether the seasonal motive was the only one, not fear of rate cuts, and the author treats the objection here as answered. A is wrong because the sentence is offered hypothetically, not as evidence.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Reyval’s study is best described as
choices: skeptical, regarding its conclusions as no better supported than those of the consensus it challenges
admiring of its methodological point but doubtful that its evidence bears on workers’ motives at all
enthusiastic, accepting both its critique of the older view and its implication that seasonal pressure fully explains restriction at Orlen Bay
largely favorable, while holding that it supports a narrower conclusion than its author sometimes implies
neutral, reporting its claims and evidence without evaluating them
questions.explanation: The author calls Reyval’s methodological point ‘well taken’ and says the study establishes something important, but also that it ‘establishes less than she sometimes suggests,’ which is D. B is the strongest trap, but it goes too far: the author grants that the pattern shows the seasonal motive was operative, so the evidence does bear on motives. C ignores the author’s point that the seasonal motive need not have been the only one.

questions.stem: The author’s claim that Reyval’s account ‘is open to a version of the same objection’ most strongly suggests that the author believes
choices: Reyval inferred workers’ motives from the bare fact of restriction without consulting the ledgers
the ledger evidence, though it reveals a pattern in workers’ conduct, cannot by itself exclude motives other than the one Reyval identifies
Reyval’s evidence concerning heavy-run years is consistent with the view that restriction was a defense against rate cuts
earlier historians were correct about the motives of workers at plants with year-round production
Reyval read her own preferences into the evidence in order to discredit the older consensus
questions.explanation: The objection was that historians read motives into behavior; the author explains that ledgers record what workers did, not why, and show the seasonal motive was operative but not that it was the only one, which is B. C is tempting because the author does criticize Reyval, but the author never disputes her answer to the rate-cut reply. A misreads the parallel: the objection is a ‘version’ of the earlier one, not an accusation that she ignored her evidence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between passage A and passage B?
choices: Passage B rejects passage A’s interpretation of a phenomenon and denies that the phenomenon confers any benefit on the trees that exhibit it.
Passage A proposes a hypothesis that passage B supports with additional, longer-term evidence.
Passage A presents data that passage B argues were improperly collected and therefore unreliable.
Passage A interprets a phenomenon as adaptive; passage B argues that the evidence for that interpretation fits a different account and that the phenomenon’s benefits may be temporary.
Passage A and passage B offer competing explanations of why droughts in a region have become more frequent.
questions.explanation: Passage A calls early shedding a defensive strategy; passage B argues that shedding usually follows leaf failure, so the stem’s benefit does not show design, and that repeated shedding can exhaust a tree’s reserves. That is D. A is the trap: passage B explicitly grants that the stem’s benefit is ‘real enough’ and that early-shedding trees often look healthier the next spring, so it does not deny any benefit.

questions.stem: According to passage A, the trees in the author’s study that shed more than half their leaves before midsummer
choices: were more likely than other trees to leaf out normally the following spring
had fewer blocked vessels in their leaves than trees that retained their foliage
died at higher rates than other trees within five years
retained larger reserves of stored starch than trees that kept their foliage
drew more water from the soil than trees that kept their foliage
questions.explanation: Passage A reports that the early-shedding trees were substantially more likely to leaf out normally the next spring, so A is correct. B is the trap: the reported difference in blocked vessels concerns trunks, not leaves. C borrows passage B’s finding about trees that shed in consecutive drought years.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following?
choices: Early leaf shedding in the pale ridge oak is not a product of natural selection.
Trunk embolisms kill more pale ridge oaks over the long term than carbon starvation does.
In a region where severe droughts occurred only rarely, early leaf shedding might on balance help pale ridge oaks survive.
Measurements of water flow in leaves are less reliable than counts of blocked vessels in trunks.
Pale ridge oaks that keep their leaves during drought suffer fewer trunk embolisms than those that shed them.
questions.explanation: Passage B says whether early leaf loss helps ‘depends on how often drought returns’ and that it ‘once bought time,’ and it grants a real short-term benefit to the stem; so with rare droughts the response could be net beneficial, as C says. A is the trap: passage B argues only that a benefit following from damage is not evidence of design, which is weaker than asserting that the trait did not evolve by selection. B contradicts B’s report that the oaks died of apparent carbon starvation rather than blocked vessels.

questions.stem: Both authors would be most likely to agree that
choices: early leaf shedding in the pale ridge oak is an evolved defensive strategy
a benefit that follows from a trait does not show that the trait arose because of that benefit
the conducting vessels of leaves are less vulnerable to blockage than those of stems
the cost of regrowing a canopy is small compared with the cost of trunk embolism
losing its leaves reduces the amount of water a tree loses during drought
questions.explanation: Passage A says shedding sharply reduces water loss, and passage B grants that the stem benefits from reduced water loss once the leaves are gone, so E is common ground. B and D each express only one author’s view (B’s and A’s respectively); indeed, passage B’s carbon-starvation findings suggest its author would doubt D. C reverses passage B’s claim about safety margins.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions that leaves have narrower margins of hydraulic safety than stems primarily in order to
choices: explain why embolisms in the trunk are difficult for trees to repair
help account for the finding that leaves had largely failed hydraulically before they were shed
suggest that the pale ridge oak is more vulnerable to drought than other tree species
support the claim that shedding leaves depletes a tree’s reserves of stored carbohydrates
concede that passage A’s description of leaves as a hydraulic fuse is correct in most cases
questions.explanation: If leaf vessels block at lower tension than stem vessels, leaves will fail first, which explains why the measured leaves had already lost most of their conductivity before falling, so B is correct. E is the trap: ‘fuse’ language might seem to fit a part that fails first, but passage B uses the point to argue that shedding follows failure rather than being a protective design, which undercuts rather than concedes A’s view.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the position taken in passage A against the objection raised in the first paragraph of passage B?
choices: In several other oak species, trees that retain their foliage through drought suffer more trunk embolisms than trees that shed it.
Leaves of pale ridge oaks that have lost most of their conducting capacity cannot regain it even if rainfall resumes before autumn.
Pale ridge oaks that shed leaves early in drought years regrow their canopies more slowly the following spring than other upland oaks do.
Drought-stressed pale ridge oaks expend energy forming a separation layer at the base of each leaf stalk, a process that begins before the leaves’ conductivity starts to decline.
The drought studied by the author of passage A was more severe than any recorded in the region in the preceding century.
questions.explanation: Passage B’s first-paragraph objection is not that shedding fails to help the stem—it grants that benefit—but that shedding merely follows leaf failure and so is a consequence, not a strategy. D shows the tree actively initiating shedding before failure begins, which directly counters that objection. A is the most tempting trap, but it supports only the stem benefit that passage B already concedes and says nothing about whether shedding is initiated or merely follows damage; B and C, if anything, help passage B.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to regard the findings reported in the second paragraph of passage A as
choices: reliable as far as they go, but unable to settle either whether shedding is a strategy or whether it benefits trees across repeated droughts
reliable, and sufficient to show that shedding is a strategy, though not that it benefits trees across repeated droughts
unreliable, because the trees that shed early had in fact lost most of their trunk conductivity
irrelevant to the dispute, because any benefit to the stem arises only after the leaves have already failed
persuasive evidence that carbon starvation is less common than trunk embolism among drought-stressed oaks
questions.explanation: Passage B accepts that early-shedding trees often look healthier the next spring and that the stem benefit is real, but argues that a benefit following damage does not show design and that one year’s survival is not a reliable measure, which is A. B is the closest trap; it accepts half of B’s position but contradicts B’s explicit claim that such a benefit is not evidence of design. D overstates: B treats the findings as showing a real but limited benefit, not as irrelevant.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because the shared-shortage rule has distributed the hardship of drought fairly, criticisms of its effects on the efficiency of water use are misplaced.

Although the shared-shortage rule has spared the basin sudden losses, it may have discouraged adaptations that strict priority would have compelled, leaving the basin less prepared for severe drought.
The shared-shortage rule should be abandoned in favor of strict priority, since only the threat of total cutoffs induces users to adapt.
The Tessaly River basin adopted the shared-shortage rule chiefly in order to protect household drinking water from reduction during shortages.
Critics of the shared-shortage rule have failed to recognize that the rule was never intended to maximize the efficiency of water use.
questions.explanation: The passage grants that the rule has prevented sudden losses but concludes that by softening every shortage it may defer a reckoning and leave the basin unprepared, which is B. C is the main trap: the author explicitly says nothing in the critics’ case shows a return to strict priority would be wise. A and E express the defenders’ reply, which the author says concedes more than intended.

questions.stem: According to the passage, under the shared-shortage rule priority dates were
choices: abolished in favor of allotments proportional to past use
used to determine which rights would be exempt from reduction
consulted to determine the order in which users would bear a shortage
retained only for rights used for household drinking water
used to resolve disputes over the size of users’ allotments
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says priority dates were consulted only to settle disputes over the size of allotments, so E is correct. C is the trap: it describes exactly the role the passage says priority dates no longer played. B confuses priority with the exemption, which depended on household drinking use.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a junior user under strict prior appropriation would be
choices: less likely than a senior user to suffer any reduction during a shortage
less likely than a junior user under the shared-shortage rule to lose his or her farm in a single dry season
more likely than a junior user under the shared-shortage rule to invest in water storage
exempt from reduction during a shortage if the water were used for household drinking
unable to calculate in advance how much water he or she would lose in a shortage
questions.explanation: Critics say the shared-shortage rule removed junior users’ strongest incentive to invest in storage—the threat of a total cutoff, which exists only under strict priority—so a junior user under strict priority would have the stronger incentive, as C says. B is the trap: it compares the right two users but in the wrong direction, since strict priority is what exposes junior farms to sudden collapse. D imports the shared-shortage rule’s exemption into strict priority, and E is false because a junior user under strict priority can foresee a total cutoff.

questions.stem: The author mentions a farmer facing a twenty percent cut primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the clarity that defenders of prior appropriation have praised
show that the shared-shortage rule imposes greater hardship on junior users than strict priority does
provide evidence that fallowing fields is the most efficient form of water conservation
illustrate why proportional reductions create weaker incentives to adapt than total cutoffs do
suggest that junior users have generally opposed the adoption of the shared-shortage rule
questions.explanation: The contrast between a farmer who can absorb a partial cut by fallowing a field and one who must find a new source or fail explains why the rule weakened incentives to invest, which is D. B reverses the comparison, since a partial cut is less harsh than a total cutoff. C misreads fallowing, which the passage presents as a way of absorbing a cut without adapting, not as efficient conservation.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the effect that critics attribute to the shared-shortage rule’s treatment of junior users?
choices: A company that responds to every decline in sales by reducing all employees’ hours slightly, instead of closing its weakest division, finds that none of its divisions has been pressed to modernize.
A city that assigns scarce parking permits by annual lottery rather than by seniority finds that residents who lose the lottery are less likely to buy cars.
A school that grades every course on a fixed curve finds that its students compete more intensely, and cooperate less, in pursuit of the highest marks.
An insurer that sharply raises premiums for drivers who have had accidents finds that its customers, on the whole, begin driving more carefully.
A fishery that assigns catch quotas according to each boat’s historical catch finds that newly built boats, however efficient, cannot profitably enter the market.
questions.explanation: Critics claim that by spreading every loss thinly the rule removed the pressure that would have forced junior users to adapt; A likewise spreads a loss so that no unit faces the pressure that would compel change, with the result that nothing modernizes. E is the most tempting trap because allocation by historical catch resembles allocation by seniority, but it corresponds to strict priority’s exclusion of newcomers, not to the rule’s blunting of incentives. D concerns a penalty that creates an incentive, the reverse of the mechanism.

questions.stem: The author of the passage would be most likely to agree with which one of the following?
choices: Strict priority would serve the Tessaly River basin better than the shared-shortage rule does.
The exemption for household drinking water is the shared-shortage rule’s principal weakness.
The aim of distributing hardship fairly was a legitimate one, but it is an aim the shared-shortage rule has failed to achieve.
The rule’s defenders are mistaken in claiming that no community in the basin has lost its farms in a single season.
The success that the rule’s defenders cite is consistent with the criticisms that have been made of the rule.
questions.explanation: The author says the defenders’ reply ‘concedes more than its proponents may intend’: the very softening of every shortage that prevents sudden losses is what may defer the reckoning, so the cited success and the criticisms are compatible, as E says. C is the strongest trap: the author does call the achievement ‘not trivial,’ but never says the rule failed to distribute hardship fairly, and does not dispute the defenders on that point. A is ruled out by the statement that nothing in the critics’ case shows a return to strict priority would be wise.

questions.stem: According to the passage, defenders of prior appropriation have praised the doctrine on the grounds that
choices: it distributes the burden of shortages evenly among all users
the security of senior rights encourages long-term investment
it prevents the sudden collapse of farms held by junior users
it exempts water used for household drinking from reduction
it makes the transfer of water to growing municipalities easier
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says defenders praise the doctrine’s clarity and the way the security of senior rights encourages long-term investment, which is B. A and C are aims of the shared-shortage rule, not merits claimed for strict priority. E is tempting because the third paragraph links the shared-shortage rule to slowed transfers, but the passage never attributes this praise to prior appropriation’s defenders.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Reductive analysis should be abandoned because its classification of notes as ornamental is circular.
Ornamentation is the most valuable element of tonal music and should be the primary focus of its analysis.
Reductive analysis remains valuable, but because its results depend on contestable choices, a reduction should be presented as one hearing of a work rather than as the work’s structure.
Performance traditions in which ornaments were improvised show that tonal music lacks any underlying structural coherence.
Although reductive analysis relies on circular reasoning, that circularity is harmless, so its results may be accepted as revealing the structure of tonal works.
questions.explanation: After raising two problems, the author concludes that reduction should be retained but understood more modestly, as one hearing shaped by choices, which is C. E is the trap: the author does say the circle is ‘not necessarily vicious,’ but then argues that because of it the skeleton is partly a product of the analyst’s expectations, so reductions should not be presented as revealing the structure. A contradicts the statement that none of this requires abandoning reduction.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A method is described, its origins are traced, and it is shown to have been superseded by a newer method.
Two competing methods are compared, and one is shown to be superior on the basis of two considerations.
A method is criticized on two grounds, those criticisms are shown to be unfounded, and the method is endorsed.
A method is described and its appeal acknowledged, two problems with it are raised, and a revised understanding of what it achieves is proposed.
A problem of interpretation is identified, a method for resolving it is introduced, and the method’s limitations are dismissed as minor.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes reduction and its appeal, the second and third raise the circularity and ornament problems, and the fourth proposes a more modest account of what reduction achieves, which is D. C is the trap because the method is retained, but the author never shows the criticisms to be unfounded; the revised account accepts them. E misdescribes the final paragraph, which takes the limitations seriously enough to change how reductions should be presented.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following?
choices: Some notes’ classification as ornamental does not depend on the analyst’s expectations about the underlying progression.
Any reduction whose classifications rely on the underlying progression is for that reason invalid.
The skeleton an analyst uncovers is entirely a product of the analyst’s prior expectations.
In traditions where performers supplied the ornaments, reductive analysis cannot be applied at all.
In analysis, the pitches a composer notated should always take precedence over notes added by performers.
questions.explanation: The author says that in many cases the classification seems obvious—a brief stepwise note between chord tones is almost universally heard as decorative—and that analysts appeal to the underlying structure only in the cases that are not obvious; so some classifications do not rest on the analyst’s expectations about the progression, which is A. C is the key degree trap: the author says the skeleton is ‘partly’ such a product, not entirely. B contradicts ‘not necessarily vicious,’ and D overstates the third paragraph, which challenges a claim about ornament’s value without saying reduction is inapplicable.

questions.stem: The author’s stance toward the claim that a reduction reveals the structure of a musical work is best described as
choices: rejection of the claim together with rejection of reductive analysis as a method
acceptance of the claim, with reservations only about how analysts classify certain notes
agnosticism, on the ground that the considerations for and against the claim are evenly balanced
acceptance of the claim for music with fixed ornaments, but rejection of it for music with improvised ornaments
rejection of the claim as stated, combined with endorsement of a weaker claim about what reduction offers
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says that ‘rather than revealing the structure of a work, a reduction offers one hearing of it,’ rejecting the strong claim while endorsing a weaker one, which is E. D is the most sophisticated trap: the ornament argument does apply specially to improvised traditions, but the circularity argument in the second paragraph applies to reduction generally, and the author’s conclusion is not limited to improvised music. A is wrong because the author says none of this requires abandoning reduction.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the circularity described in the second paragraph of the passage?
