choices: A translator renders each of a poem’s idioms word for word, so that the finished translation is literally faithful to the original but awkward to read.
A historian assumes, without examining the matter, that the most recent document in an archive is the most reliable account of the event it describes.
An editor reconstructs an author’s original text by discarding readings judged to be copyists’ errors, and judges readings to be errors because they do not fit the text as reconstructed.
A critic evaluates a novel solely by comparing it with the other novels its author has written, ignoring the work of the author’s contemporaries.
A mapmaker leaves the minor roads off a regional map so that travelers can more easily see the major highways connecting its cities.
questions.explanation: In the passage, ornament is identified as what does not belong to the underlying progression, while the progression is identified by setting aside ornament; C has the same mutual dependence between the errors and the reconstructed text. E is the attractive trap because it involves simplifying by stripping away lesser details, but the mapmaker’s judgment of which roads are minor does not depend on the map that results, so there is no circle. B involves an unexamined assumption but not mutual dependence.

questions.stem: The author refers to performance traditions in which performers supplied the ornaments primarily in order to
choices: show that reductive analysis cannot explain how long movements are heard as coherent wholes
challenge the assumption that ornamentation is by its nature inessential to a musical work
provide an example of a case in which classifying a note as ornamental is obvious
argue that performers rather than composers should be regarded as the authors of tonal works
illustrate the circular reasoning described in the second paragraph
questions.explanation: Because listeners in those traditions judged performances chiefly by their ornamentation, treating ornament as inessential becomes a substantive and possibly mistaken claim about value, so the example challenges that assumption, as B says. E is the trap: the example follows the discussion of circularity, but the third paragraph introduces it as a ‘further difficulty,’ distinct from the circle. D overstates a point about where value lies into a claim about authorship.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the author recommends that analysts who use reduction
choices: state their reasons for every note they classify as ornamental
give up the search for a skeleton that underlies an entire work
study the performance practices of a work’s original audiences before analyzing it
explain why they classified a note as they did wherever that classification is in dispute
present several alternative reductions of each work so that listeners can choose among them
questions.explanation: The final paragraph recommends stating, ‘wherever the classification of a note is contested, why they classified it as they did,’ which is D. A is the key trap: it uses the passage’s own idea but broadens it from contested classifications to every classification, which the author does not recommend and which the second paragraph’s point about obvious cases makes unnecessary. E is a plausible extension of ‘one hearing’ but is never recommended.

questions.stimulus: Darvale’s housing council predicts that relaxing the city’s restrictions on backyard cottages will noticeably lower rents. This prediction is unlikely to be borne out. Admittedly, any new housing adds to supply, and added supply tends to restrain prices. But in cities that have already relaxed such restrictions, most new backyard cottages have been occupied by the owners’ relatives or listed as short-term vacation rentals. Units used in these ways do little to expand the stock of housing available to ordinary long-term renters.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Units occupied by owners’ relatives or used as vacation rentals do little to expand the housing available to long-term renters.
Adding to the supply of housing generally tends to restrain the prices of housing.
Relaxing Darvale’s restrictions on backyard cottages probably will not noticeably lower the city’s rents.
Darvale’s housing council should not relax the city’s restrictions on backyard cottages.
Most backyard cottages built in Darvale will be occupied by the owners’ relatives.
questions.explanation: The argument’s point is that the council’s prediction of lower rents is unlikely to come true, which C restates; everything else is offered in support of that. A is a premise supporting the conclusion, and B is a concession. D goes further than the argument, which never says the restrictions should stay in place.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: In a thorough survey of the Pellam Valley, we located 340 hives of the blue mason bee, and every one of them was within 200 meters of a stand of wild sage. Since wild sage grows in scattered stands across nearly the entire valley floor, the bees evidently have no trouble finding sites near it. Plainly, then, in the Pellam Valley it is the presence of wild sage that determines where blue mason bees build their hives.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to establish that the bees’ hive sites are any closer to wild sage than randomly chosen locations in the valley would be
draws a conclusion about the valley’s bees from a sample of hives that may not be representative of them
presupposes the truth of the very conclusion that it is attempting to establish
fails to consider that some hives may also have been located near plants other than wild sage
treats a condition that is necessary for hive building as though it were sufficient for it
questions.explanation: If sage stands are scattered across nearly the whole valley, almost any spot would lie within 200 meters of one, so the correlation reveals nothing about the bees’ choice of sites (A). B is the trap, but the survey was thorough and the conclusion is limited to the valley, so representativeness is not the problem. D is irrelevant, since nearness to other plants would not show that sage plays no role.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, forecasters at the Hollin weather station have noted that mornings with a southerly wind pattern known locally as the ‘lift’ are followed by afternoon thunderstorms far more often than are other mornings. The station’s lead meteorologist contends that the lift itself produces these storms: it pushes warm, moist air from the lowlands up the slopes of the nearby hills, where the air cools and its moisture condenses into storm clouds.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the meteorologist’s argument?
choices: Afternoon thunderstorms also occur near Hollin on some days when the lift has not occurred that morning.
Weather stations in other regions rarely record a morning wind pattern resembling the lift.
The lift is most common in midsummer, when afternoon thunderstorms near Hollin are most common in general.
Forecasts issued by the Hollin station have become more accurate over the past decade.
On mornings when the lift occurs but the lowland air is unusually dry, afternoon thunderstorms near Hollin are rare.
questions.explanation: The meteorologist’s proposed mechanism depends on the lift carrying moist air uphill; if storms fail to follow the lift precisely when the lowland air is dry, that is just what the mechanism predicts (E). C weakens the argument by suggesting that season, not the lift, explains the correlation. A is compatible with the argument, since the lift need not be the only cause of storms.

questions.stimulus:
Imogen: The editors of the new anthology were right to exclude poems written in strict traditional forms. Most readers today find the sonnet and the villanelle stiff and artificial, and an anthology aimed at a general audience ought to feature work that its readers will find natural and engaging.

Teodor: An anthology that presents itself as a survey of contemporary poetry has an obligation to represent that poetry accurately, and several of the most admired poets working today write in strict forms. Whatever readers’ tastes may be, leaving such poems out misrepresents the field.
questions.stem: Imogen and Teodor disagree over whether
choices: most readers today find traditional poetic forms stiff and artificial
the anthology’s editors were justified in excluding poems written in strict traditional forms
several of the most admired contemporary poets write in strict forms
an anthology aimed at a general audience should include at least some poems in free verse
poems in strict traditional forms are more difficult to write than poems in free verse
questions.explanation: Imogen says the editors were right to exclude strict-form poems; Teodor says the exclusion misrepresents the field and so was a mistake (B). Teodor never disputes A (‘whatever readers’ tastes may be’), and Imogen never addresses C. Neither speaker discusses D or E.

questions.stimulus: Each drug tested in the Corvane trial that reduced inflammation also raised blood pressure in at least some of the patients who took it. No drug tested in the trial was later approved for use in elderly patients unless it raised blood pressure in none of the patients who took it. Some of the drugs tested in the trial were later approved for use in elderly patients, and most of those drugs were also approved for use in children.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: None of the drugs tested in the trial that were approved for use in children reduced inflammation.
Some of the drugs tested in the trial that were approved for elderly patients reduced inflammation.
Most of the drugs tested in the trial that raised no patient’s blood pressure were approved for elderly patients.
At least one drug tested in the trial that was approved for use in children did not reduce inflammation.
At least one drug tested in the trial raised blood pressure in some of the patients who took it.
questions.explanation: Any drug approved for elderly patients raised no one’s blood pressure and therefore did not reduce inflammation; since some such drugs exist and most of them were approved for children, at least one child-approved drug did not reduce inflammation (D). A is the trap: drugs approved for children but not for elderly patients are unconstrained, so some could have reduced inflammation. E need not hold, since perhaps no drug reduced inflammation and none raised blood pressure.

questions.stimulus: Manager: Last year our firm began allowing employees in its design department to work from home two days a week. Since then, the number of projects the design department completes each month has risen by 15 percent. Clearly, allowing employees to work from home increases their productivity, so we should extend the policy to every department in the firm.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the manager’s argument?
choices: A few employees in the design department chose not to work from home even after the policy took effect.
Shortly after the policy took effect, the design department hired four additional designers, enlarging its staff by 20 percent.
Employees in several of the firm’s other departments have said that they would like to work from home.
The projects completed by the design department last year were, on average, no smaller than those completed the year before.
Some of the firm’s managers believe that remote work makes employees more difficult to supervise.
questions.explanation: If the department’s staff grew by 20 percent while output grew by only 15 percent, output per employee actually fell, so the rise in completed projects does not show that remote work boosted productivity (B). D rules out an alternative explanation and so slightly strengthens the argument. A and E have little bearing on whether the policy raised productivity.

questions.stimulus: Legislator: The proposed tax credit for residential rooftop solar panels will reduce our state’s reliance on coal-fired power. The credit will lead many homeowners to install solar panels, and the electricity those panels generate will replace electricity the homeowners would otherwise have drawn from the power grid. At present, coal-fired plants supply the majority of the electricity on our state’s grid.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the legislator’s argument depends?
choices: Most homeowners who install solar panels after the credit takes effect would not have installed them without it.
Electricity from rooftop solar panels is less expensive to produce than electricity from coal-fired plants.
The tax credit will not significantly reduce the revenue available to the state government.
Coal-fired plants will continue to supply the majority of the electricity on the state’s grid for at least the next decade.
A reduction in the demand for electricity from the grid would lead to at least some reduction in the output of coal-fired plants.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from less demand for grid power to less reliance on coal; if reduced demand were met entirely by cutting output from other sources, coal use would not fall, so E is required. A is too strong: the argument needs only that some homeowners install panels because of the credit. D is also not needed, since coal could lose its majority and still have its output reduced.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, the Fernhill Public Library eliminated the fines it had charged for overdue books. Since then, the percentage of borrowed books that are returned after their due date has increased slightly. Over the same period, however, the number of borrowed books that are never returned at all has dropped substantially, even though the library has not changed its other policies for recovering unreturned books.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many borrowers who used to keep overdue books indefinitely did so to avoid paying the large fines that had accumulated on them.
Other libraries in the region that have eliminated overdue fines have also seen an increase in late returns.
The Fernhill Public Library has hired additional staff to process returned books more quickly.
The number of people borrowing books from the Fernhill Public Library has increased since fines were eliminated.
The fines the library had charged for overdue books had generated a substantial portion of its revenue.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why eliminating fines would make lateness more common but permanent non-return less common. A explains it: fines had deterred people from ever returning badly overdue books, so removing them brought those books back late rather than never. B explains only the rise in late returns, and D would, if anything, increase both figures rather than explain why one fell.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: Some physicians have warned patients with high blood pressure to avoid the cold remedy Brevane. This warning, however, is unwarranted. Brevane contains three active ingredients, and in controlled studies each of them, taken alone at the dose found in Brevane, produced no measurable rise in blood pressure, even among patients whose blood pressure was poorly controlled. Since Brevane consists of nothing more than these three ingredients plus inert fillers, it too poses no risk to such patients.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the pharmacist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: rejects the physicians’ warning on the basis of their presumed motives rather than its merits
generalizes to all patients with high blood pressure from studies of patients whose blood pressure was poorly controlled
presumes that because each component of a product is harmless when taken in isolation, the product as a whole is harmless
overlooks the possibility that the fillers in Brevane, though inert, could themselves raise blood pressure
mistakes a factor that is merely associated with high blood pressure for a cause of it
questions.explanation: Each ingredient was tested only alone; the ingredients might interact to raise blood pressure when combined, so what holds of each part need not hold of the whole (C). B is the main trap, but studying patients with poorly controlled blood pressure makes the evidence stronger rather than weaker for other patients. D contradicts a premise the argument states, namely that the fillers are inert.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A manager should publicly credit an individual employee for a team’s success only if that employee’s contribution was both essential to the success and substantially greater than that of any other member of the team.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Okafor acted properly in publicly crediting Lin for the success of the product launch, since Lin’s work was essential to it, even though two other team members contributed just as much.
Hale acted improperly in failing to publicly credit Marsh for the success of the audit, since Marsh’s contribution was essential and far exceeded that of any other team member.

Brandt acted properly in publicly crediting Yusuf for the success of the merger, since Yusuf contributed far more than anyone else, even though the merger would have succeeded without that contribution.
Ruiz acted improperly in publicly crediting Dalton for the success of the campaign, since although Dalton’s work was indispensable, Pereira’s contribution was equally large.
Singh acted improperly in publicly crediting the entire team, rather than any single member, for the success of the redesign.
questions.explanation: The principle states two necessary conditions for crediting an individual; in D, Dalton’s contribution was not greater than Pereira’s, so crediting Dalton violated the principle and the judgment of impropriety conforms. B is the trap: the principle gives only necessary conditions for crediting someone, so it never requires crediting anyone and cannot show Hale acted improperly. A and C approve credit when one of the conditions fails, and E concerns team credit, which the principle does not address.

questions.stimulus: In the Marrow Basin, fog forms only on nights when the ground cools enough that the air just above it reaches its dew point, the temperature at which water vapor condenses. Cloud cover at night slows the cooling of the ground by trapping heat radiated from the surface. Over the past twenty years, the average amount of nighttime cloud cover over the basin has increased substantially, while the average humidity of the basin’s air has remained essentially unchanged.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Over the past twenty years, nights on which fog forms in the Marrow Basin have probably become less frequent.
Fog never forms in the Marrow Basin on nights when there is substantial cloud cover.
The humidity of the air is the most important factor in determining whether fog forms in the Marrow Basin.
The increase in nighttime cloud cover over the Marrow Basin has been caused by changes in the region’s climate.
Days following foggy nights in the Marrow Basin tend to be cooler than days following clear nights.
questions.explanation: More cloud cover means the ground cools less at night, and with humidity unchanged, the air will reach its dew point less often, so fog has probably become less frequent (A). B is too strong, since clouds only slow cooling and do not prevent it. C and D make claims about relative importance and about causes that the passage does not address.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Every poem in Halloran’s new collection, except the prose poems, relies heavily on enjambment, the running of a sentence past the end of a line without a pause. Any poem that relies heavily on enjambment loses much of its effect when read aloud, because listeners cannot hear where the lines end. And each of the collection’s prose poems runs longer than ten pages. It follows that none of the poems in Halloran’s new collection is suitable for a public reading.
questions.stem: The critic’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any poem that loses much of its effect when read aloud is unsuitable for a public reading.
A poem is suitable for a public reading if it neither loses much of its effect when read aloud nor runs longer than ten pages.
No prose poem that runs longer than ten pages relies heavily on enjambment.
Most poems that run longer than ten pages lose much of their effect when read aloud.
A poem is suitable for a public reading only if it does not lose much of its effect when read aloud and does not run longer than ten pages.
questions.explanation: E says that losing effect aloud or running over ten pages each rules a poem out; the non-prose poems lose effect aloud and the prose poems run over ten pages, so every poem is ruled out. A is the trap: it rules out the enjambed poems but says nothing about the prose poems. B reverses the conditional, giving conditions for suitability rather than for unsuitability, and D is only a ‘most’ claim about length.

questions.stimulus: Some researchers attribute the recent decline of the Ashby firefly to pesticide runoff from nearby farms. This explanation, however, is inadequate. The firefly has declined just as sharply within the Ashby nature reserve, where pesticides have been banned for decades, as on the surrounding farmland. A more likely culprit is artificial light. Ashby fireflies locate mates by means of their flashes, and both the reserve and the farmland have seen a dramatic increase in nighttime light from nearby housing developments over the same period.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the firefly has declined just as sharply within the reserve as on the surrounding farmland?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
It is used to undermine a rival hypothesis by showing that the decline occurs even where the factor that hypothesis cites is absent.
It is a hypothesis that the argument considers and ultimately endorses.
It is presented as evidence that the factor the argument favors is at work in both the reserve and the farmland.
It is a claim that the argument concedes but maintains is irrelevant to its conclusion.
questions.explanation: The equal decline inside a reserve where pesticides are banned shows that the pesticide hypothesis, which the argument rejects, cannot account for the decline (B). D is the trap: the rise in nighttime light in both places is established by a separate, later claim, and the claim in question says nothing about light. The claim is a premise, not the main conclusion (A) or a hypothesis (C).

questions.stimulus: Economist: In Brayton, the new rule requiring that 15 percent of the units in large new apartment buildings be rented at below-market rates has caused a slowdown in residential construction. In the two years since the rule took effect, applications for permits to build large apartment buildings in Brayton have fallen by 40 percent compared with the two years before the rule took effect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the economist’s argument?
choices: Several developers who build large apartment buildings in Brayton have publicly criticized the rule.
Permit applications for small apartment buildings, which are exempt from the rule, have increased in Brayton since the rule took effect.
The rule was announced well before it took effect, and developers rushed to file applications before the effective date so that their projects would be exempt.
Apartments rented at below-market rates in Brayton have long waiting lists of prospective tenants.
Large apartment buildings in Brayton typically take more than two years to complete once a permit application has been filed.
questions.explanation: C attacks the comparison rather than the conclusion: if developers rushed applications into the period just before the rule took effect, the baseline is inflated and much of the 40 percent drop reflects shifted timing rather than a real slowdown. B is a tempting trap but actually strengthens the argument, since unregulated building kept growing. E concerns completion time, which does not affect the count of applications filed.

questions.stimulus: Archivist: Some people argue that because digital scans make the contents of fragile manuscripts widely accessible, libraries no longer need to devote resources to preserving the original documents. But if this reasoning were sound, then the existence of detailed photographs of a historic building would mean that there was no need to preserve the building itself. No one would accept that conclusion, since a building, like a manuscript, contains information about its materials, its construction, and its history of use that no image can fully capture.
questions.stem: The archivist’s argument proceeds by
choices: questioning the motives of those who advance the view being criticized
offering evidence that digital scans of manuscripts are frequently inaccurate
presenting a single counterexample to a generalization about all manuscripts
showing that similar reasoning, applied to an analogous case, would lead to an unacceptable conclusion
demonstrating that the opposing view’s conclusion contradicts one of its own premises
questions.explanation: The archivist applies the opponents’ reasoning to buildings and photographs, notes that the resulting conclusion is clearly unacceptable, and so rejects the original reasoning (D). C is tempting, but the building case is an analogy, not a manuscript that contradicts a generalization. The archivist never claims scans are inaccurate (B) or discusses motives (A).

questions.stimulus: Every house in the Ostrand historic district that was built before 1920 has a slate roof, unless it was substantially rebuilt after a fire. The Whitcomb house stands in the Ostrand district and does not have a slate roof, but it has never been substantially rebuilt after a fire. Therefore, the Whitcomb house was not built before 1920.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every painting in the Harrow collection that was acquired before 1900 has been restored, unless it is on long-term loan. The portrait of Ada Venn is in the Harrow collection and has not been restored. Therefore, it was not acquired before 1900.

Every tenor in the Greenleaf choir attends the Thursday rehearsal, unless excused by the director. Paulo, a member of the choir, attends the Thursday rehearsal and has not been excused. Therefore, Paulo sings tenor.

Every bridge in Dunmore County that was built before 1950 has been inspected this year, unless it is closed to traffic. The Mill Road bridge is in Dunmore County and has not been inspected this year. Therefore, it either was not built before 1950 or is closed to traffic.

No vehicle in the city fleet that runs on diesel is more than ten years old, unless it has been overhauled. The street sweeper is in the fleet, is more than ten years old, and has been overhauled. Therefore, it runs on diesel.

Every restaurant on Cole Street that opened last year serves breakfast, unless it lacks a full kitchen. The Bluebird Café is on Cole Street and does not serve breakfast, but it has a full kitchen. Therefore, the Bluebird Café did not open last year.
questions.explanation: The original: every member of a group with feature X has feature Y unless exception Z; this member lacks Y and lacks Z; so it lacks X. E matches every element. A is the main trap but never rules out the exception (the loan), so its conclusion does not follow. C is valid but never eliminates the exception, so it reaches a disjunctive conclusion instead; B and D reverse the logic.

questions.stimulus: Utility spokesperson: Critics of the proposed Grisham Ridge wind farm claim that it will force the utility to raise its electricity rates. But under state regulations, the utility may raise its rates only if its operating costs increase, and the wind farm will reduce those costs. After all, wind turbines require no fuel, and fuel purchases are by far the largest component of the utility’s current operating costs. So the critics’ claim is mistaken.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the spokesperson’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that savings in one component of a total will not be offset by increases in its other components
treats a condition that is necessary for the utility to raise its rates as though it were sufficient
rejects the critics’ claim on the basis of the critics’ presumed motives rather than its merits
fails to consider that the state might revise its regulations governing electricity rates
assumes that fuel purchases will remain the largest component of the utility’s costs after the wind farm is built
questions.explanation: Cutting fuel purchases reduces operating costs only if the wind farm does not add other operating costs, such as maintenance and transmission, that exceed the fuel savings (A). B is the trap: the argument uses the regulation correctly, moving from costs not increasing to rates not rising, which is a valid contrapositive. E is not needed, since fuel can lose its top ranking and the argument is unaffected.

questions.stimulus: Researchers gave patients who suffer from chronic migraines either the drug Tolvarin or a placebo for six months. Patients receiving Tolvarin reported 40 percent fewer migraines than those receiving the placebo. Tolvarin, however, produces a distinctive metallic taste that most patients notice within a few days. Nevertheless, the researchers conclude that Tolvarin reduces the frequency of migraines through its pharmacological action and not merely through patients’ expectations about the drug.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers’ argument?
choices: Most patients in the Tolvarin group correctly guessed, partway through the study, that they were receiving the drug.
In an earlier study using a taste-masked form of Tolvarin, patients reported fewer migraines after six months than before treatment began.
Patients in the Tolvarin group who never noticed the metallic taste reported reductions in migraines as large as those reported by patients who noticed it.
The metallic taste produced by Tolvarin fades for most patients after the first few weeks of treatment.
Tolvarin is chemically similar to a drug that is widely used to lower blood pressure.
questions.explanation: The worry is that the taste tipped patients off and their expectations, not the drug, reduced the migraines. Patients who never noticed the taste had no such cue, so their equal improvement points to the drug itself (C). B is the most tempting trap, but without a placebo comparison a before-and-after improvement could reflect expectation or natural variation. D does not help, because expectations formed in the early weeks could persist after the taste fades, and A weakens the argument.

questions.stimulus: Consultant: At Pelham Logistics, warehouse teams whose members hold a brief meeting at the start of each shift have markedly lower error rates than teams that skip such meetings. Currently, about half of Pelham’s warehouse teams hold these meetings voluntarily. Therefore, if Pelham’s management requires every warehouse team to hold a start-of-shift meeting, the company’s overall warehouse error rate will decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the consultant’s argument?
choices: Teams that hold start-of-shift meetings have lower error rates than other teams on every type of warehouse task.
Start-of-shift meetings would reduce errors at least somewhat even among teams that hold them only because they are required to.
The lower error rates of teams that hold start-of-shift meetings are due entirely to the meetings and not to any other difference between those teams and the rest.
Start-of-shift meetings are the most effective means available to Pelham for reducing warehouse errors.
Pelham’s overall warehouse error rate is higher than that of comparable logistics companies.
questions.explanation: The teams that would newly hold meetings would do so only under compulsion; if meetings held that way did nothing, the overall rate would not fall, so B is required. C is the strongest trap: the argument needs the meetings to account for some of the difference, not all of it, so ‘entirely’ makes C stronger than necessary. A and D are likewise more than the argument needs.

questions.stimulus: At the Kestrel Point weather station, every day last March on which the barometric pressure fell by more than 5 millibars was immediately followed by a day on which measurable rain fell. On no day last March on which measurable rain fell did the high temperature at Kestrel Point exceed 12°C. Moreover, every day last March that immediately followed a day with a high temperature above 12°C was a day on which the barometric pressure fell by more than 5 millibars.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: The high temperatures at Kestrel Point on both March 10 and March 11 exceeded 12°C.
Measurable rain fell at Kestrel Point on March 20, and the high temperature there on March 21 exceeded 12°C.
On March 31, the pressure at Kestrel Point fell by more than 5 millibars, and the high temperature there that day was 14°C.
The high temperatures at Kestrel Point on both March 10 and March 12 exceeded 12°C.
On every day last March on which the high temperature exceeded 12°C, the pressure fell by less than 5 millibars.
questions.explanation: A high above 12°C on March 10 means the pressure fell by more than 5 millibars on March 11, which means rain on March 12, which means March 12’s high could not exceed 12°C; so D is impossible. A is the main trap, but the chain from March 10 constrains only March 12, so March 11 can also be warm. C is possible because the rules constrain the day after a pressure drop, not the day of the drop, and E is consistent as long as each warm day is followed by a cooler day with a pressure drop.

questions.stimulus: The Westbrook Library board should not remove the novel Gallows Field from the library’s young-adult section, even though several parents have complained that the book’s themes are too dark for teenagers. A panel of teachers and librarians, all experienced in evaluating literature for young readers, reviewed the novel at the board’s request and unanimously judged it appropriate for teenage readers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: A library should give the judgments of parents priority over those of other community members when deciding which books to offer to young readers.
A library should acquire the books that are most frequently requested by the patrons it is intended to serve.
A library should keep in its young-adult section any book that qualified evaluators have judged to be of high literary quality.
A library board should consult teachers before acquiring any new book for its young-adult section.
A library should not remove a book on account of objections to its themes if qualified evaluators have judged it appropriate for the readers for whom it is shelved.
questions.explanation: The argument rejects removal despite objections to the book’s themes, on the grounds that qualified evaluators judged it appropriate for teenagers; E connects exactly those elements. C is the trap: it hinges on literary quality, but the panel judged the book’s appropriateness for teenagers, not its quality. A would support removal, and B and D concern acquiring books rather than removing them.

questions.stimulus: Energy analyst: Under state law, any power plant that the Varden Commission certifies as low-emission qualifies for the state’s carbon credit, and the Tessaly power plant does not qualify for that credit. Moreover, every plant that uses the new oxide-scrubbing process emits less sulfur than the state limit allows. So we can conclude that the Tessaly plant does not use the new oxide-scrubbing process.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the analyst’s conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: The Varden Commission certifies as low-emission every power plant that emits less sulfur than the state limit allows.
Every power plant that the Varden Commission certifies as low-emission emits less sulfur than the state limit allows.
Some power plants that use the new oxide-scrubbing process do not qualify for the state’s carbon credit.
No power plant that emits more sulfur than the state limit allows qualifies for the state’s carbon credit.
The Tessaly plant emits more sulfur than does any power plant that the Varden Commission has certified as low-emission.
questions.explanation: With A, the chain runs: uses the process, so emits below the limit, so is certified, so qualifies for the credit. Since Tessaly does not qualify, it cannot use the process. B reverses the needed link and so leaves the chain broken. D tells us only about plants above the limit, and E compares Tessaly to certified plants without tying it to the sulfur limit, so neither guarantees the conclusion. C, if anything, conflicts with the chain the argument needs.

questions.stimulus: At the Linden apiary, honeybee colonies whose hives were treated with the miticide Varomex had far fewer parasitic mites by autumn than untreated colonies. Varomex kills mites riding on adult bees, but it does not reach mites developing inside sealed brood cells, where young bees mature. Colonies treated in late summer, when the rearing of young bees is minimal, showed much larger reductions in mites by autumn than did colonies treated in early summer.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Treating a colony with Varomex in early summer does not reduce the colony’s mite population by autumn.
Untreated colonies at the Linden apiary had more mites by autumn because they reared more young bees.
In early summer, a substantial proportion of the mites in a colony are inside sealed brood cells.
Mites can reproduce only inside the sealed brood cells of a honeybee colony.
Treating colonies with Varomex in both early and late summer would eliminate their mites entirely.
questions.explanation: Varomex misses mites in sealed brood cells, and early-summer treatment, when brood rearing is substantial, worked much less well than late-summer treatment; the best explanation is that many mites are sheltered in brood cells in early summer (C). A is too strong, since early-summer treatment produced smaller reductions, not none. D and E go well beyond the information given.

questions.stimulus: Most of the poets who won the Larkspur Prize during the past decade studied at the Avenell Writers’ Workshop. And most of the poets who have studied at the Avenell Writers’ Workshop write primarily in free verse. So most of the poets who won the Larkspur Prize during the past decade write primarily in free verse.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: All of the houses on Birch Lane were built by Ostler Homes, and all houses built by Ostler Homes have finished basements. So all of the houses on Birch Lane have finished basements.
Most of the tenants in the Calloway building own pets, and most pet owners in the city prefer ground-floor apartments. So most of the tenants in the Calloway building prefer ground-floor apartments.
Most of the dishes on the restaurant’s menu contain garlic, and some dishes that contain garlic are spicy. So some of the dishes on the restaurant’s menu are probably spicy.
Most of the members of the hiking club are retired, and no one who is retired works full-time. So most of the members of the hiking club do not work full-time.
Most voters in the district support the school levy, and the levy’s strongest supporters are homeowners. So most voters in the district are homeowners.
questions.explanation: The original chains two ‘most’ statements: most A are B, most B are C, so most A are C. This is invalid because the A’s that are B might fall among the B’s that are not C. B commits exactly this error. A and D are valid arguments (all-all and most-none), C uses ‘some’ with a hedged conclusion, and E commits a different error by inferring a group’s makeup from who its strongest supporters are.

questions.stimulus: Real estate analyst: In Carrow County, the proportion of home sales in which the buyer came from out of state rose from 10 percent in 2020 to 25 percent in 2024. Some observers have dismissed this as a statistical blip, but a change of this size, sustained over four years, cannot be dismissed so easily. It follows that fewer homes in Carrow County were sold to in-state buyers in 2024 than in 2020.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the analyst’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that out-of-state buyers pay higher prices for homes than in-state buyers do
presumes without justification that the rise in out-of-state buyers was caused by competition with in-state buyers
relies on data from too short a period to establish a trend in the county’s housing market
overlooks the possibility that the total number of home sales in the county increased substantially
fails to consider that some out-of-state buyers may have moved to Carrow County after buying homes there
questions.explanation: A falling share of sales to in-state buyers is compatible with a rising number of such sales if total sales grew enough; 75 percent of a much larger market can exceed 90 percent of a smaller one (D). B is a trap, since the argument draws no causal conclusion about competition at all. E is tempting but irrelevant, because the conclusion concerns who the buyers were when the homes were sold.
